title: Profit Maximization Across Market Structures

learningObjectives.text: Know and understand the following economic terms: marginal analysis, marginal benefit, marginal cost, marginal revenue, monopoly, monopolistic competition, perfectly competitive market
Be able to identify when a firm operates in an industry that is perfectly competitive, monopolistically competitive, or a monopoly
Be able to identify the sources of (and strategies for obtaining) monopoly power
Know how to calculate the profit-maximizing levels of price and quantity for perfectly competitive, monopolistically competitive, and monopoly firms using marginal analysis

keyTerms.def: Deciding by comparing the benefit and cost of one more unit: keep going until the marginal benefit (MB) equals the marginal cost (MC). MB = MC.
The additional benefit (e.g., revenue) from one more unit of an activity.
keyTerms.src: S10 slides p.15 (table); wording GENERAL ECON

keyTerms.def: The additional cost of one more unit (dC/dQ).
keyTerms.src: S06 Video p.20; S10 slides p.15

keyTerms.def: The additional revenue collected when one additional unit of production or service is rendered. MR = dR/dQ.

Many firms; homogeneous goods (commodities); perfect information: yes; transaction costs: no; free entry/exit: yes; no influence on price (price taker); D_firm = P_market = MR; Q* where P_market = MC(Q*); P* = P_market.
Many firms; differentiated goods (fast food); perfect information: no; transaction costs: yes; free entry/exit: yes; price maker; faces its own D_firm; Q* where MR(Q*) = MC(Q*); P* = P(Q*).
One firm (e.g., rural gas station); price maker; D_firm = D_market; Q* where MR(Q*) = MC(Q*); P* = P(Q*). Information, transaction costs, entry: N/A in the professor's table.
A price taker has no influence on price (perfect competition); a price maker sets price from its downward-sloping demand (monopoly, monopolistic competition).

formulas.name: Marginal revenue
formulas.latex: MR = \frac{dR}{dQ},\quad P = a - bQ \Rightarrow R = aQ - bQ^2,\; MR = a - 2bQ

workedExamples.name: Advertising spend
workedExamples.answer: MB falls 90→0, MC rises 10→100; MB = MC = 50 at 5 ads; profit peaks at 200 (4 or 5 ads)

workedExamples.name: MR from inverse demand
workedExamples.answer: R = 10Q − Q², MR = 10 − 2Q; revenue peaks at Q = 5 (R = 25) where MR = 0

workedExamples.name: Price taker at $40
workedExamples.answer: MR = P = 40, MC = 8Q → Q* = 5; C = 225; R = 200; profit = −25. Operate in the short run, exit in the long run.

workedExamples.name: Monopoly
workedExamples.answer: MR = 100 − 2Q = 8Q → Q* = 10; P* = 90; C = 525; R = 900; profit = 375. Will not face entry unless patents/entry barriers are eliminated.

workedExamples.name: Monopolistic competition
workedExamples.givens: Same cost; P = 100 − Q for your brand
workedExamples.answer: Short run identical to monopoly: Q = 10, P = 90, profit 375 (ATC 52.5). Long run: imitators enter, demand shifts to P = 50 − Q; tangency at Q = 5, P = ATC = 45, profit = 0.

workedExamples.name: Provo Peaks Root Beer (midterm practice)
workedExamples.givens: 350 obs, 7 states; Q (cases) on price ($) and income ($000/capita)
workedExamples.answer: Q = 200.152 − 5.849P + 7.804I; price t −2.151 p 0.032 (significant); income t 6.677 p 0.000 (significant, normal good); R² 0.122 (only 12.2% of variation explained); F 24.065

traps: Price taker: MR = P (horizontal demand), so set P = MC
Price maker: find Q from MR = MC FIRST, then read P off demand (not off MC)
MR has twice the slope of linear inverse demand
Negative profit in the short run ≠ shut down; long-run exit
Monopolistic competition: short-run profit is competed away in the long run (P = ATC)
Profit = R − C including fixed cost
